lead: A VR system has three output channels: visual, auditory and haptic. Each channel needs a display that turns numbers in the scene into a signal the body can sense. The right device is not the most expensive one. It is the cheapest device that meets the task's real numbers: field of view, angular resolution, latency, update rate, users, mobility, hygiene and cost. This chapter gives the output half of the system block diagram, the units for each selection number, and a weighted scoring method. The worked example uses a fixed rupee budget.
prereq: You need Unit 1: components of a VR system, the Three I's, and VR versus 3D computer graphics, plus the display families in 3.3.

blocks.text: Output devices form the half of the VR system that faces the user's senses. The digital scene goes to three displays: a graphics display makes a 2D image for the eye, a sound display makes sound at the two ears, and a haptic display makes force or skin deformation on the body. The input half, trackers and controllers, measures the user; see Unit 2, Input Devices and Tracking.

Visual output is the most demanding channel. A head-mounted display must fill a wide field of view and keep angular resolution high while the head turns. Sound output is easier to satisfy: headphones can place cues at each ear, as the chapter on 3D sound displays explains. Haptic output is split by body part, as the chapter on haptic displays explains. A tracker is an input device; a display is an output device. Swapping them is a common diagram error.
Selection uses measurable numbers. Write each number with its unit before comparing products.

items: Field of view (degrees): the angle the display covers. A wider field of view fills more of the viewer's natural view.
Angular resolution (pixels per degree, ppd): pixels per degree of view. Higher ppd means a sharper image at the same field of view.
Latency (ms): delay from a head movement to the matching image. Lower is better.
Update rate (Hz): images per second. Higher update rate gives smoother motion. Hz means cycles per second.
Stereo or mono: stereo sends one image to each eye; mono sends the same image to both.
Head tracking: the display follows head orientation. A head-mounted display needs it; a fixed monitor does not.
Simultaneous users: how many people can view or interact at one time.
Mobility: fixed room equipment or a wearable unit.
Hygiene: shared face contact and cleaning effort.

blocks.text: A single number can hide a bad choice. 1920×1080 total pixels on a large monitor can be less sharp than 2160×2160 per eye on a head-mounted display, because sharpness depends on ppd, not total pixels alone.
Some syllabi call this choosing output devices for 3D user interfaces. A weighted score makes the trade-offs visible.

items: List the requirements with units, such as six users, head motion, 20 ppd, 20 ms latency and 5,00,000 rupees.
Remove any candidate that fails a must-have, such as budget or user count.
Give each remaining requirement a weight w from 0 to 1; all weights sum to 1.
Score each candidate s from 0 to 5 on each requirement.
Compute S = Σ wᵢ sᵢ. Higher S is better. Keep cost as a hard limit unless you score it too.

blocks.where: S is the total weighted score; wᵢ is the weight of requirement i, from 0 to 1; sᵢ is the candidate's score on requirement i, from 0 to 5; the sum runs over all requirements.

sections.h3: The eye and hand set the budget

blocks.text: The eye and hand are far more demanding than the ear. A small sound timing error is tolerated in many tasks. A visual lag or a weak force cue is noticed at once. So visual and haptic choice drives the budget. Spend on the display and the haptic device first. Use headphones or simple speakers for the audio channel, and link that choice to 3D sound displays.

The task decides the split. A walkthrough for many viewers needs a large display; a surgical rehearsal needs head motion and hand force; a desk design review needs stereo and fine hand control. Audio rarely changes the shortlist. Cost is not the only limit: space, power, cleaning time and staff training also count. A cheap device that needs a dark room or daily calibration can cost more over a semester, so put recurring costs in the same budget line.

figure.caption: The worked example as a running budget. After the stereo monitor and the head display, ₹50,000 is left; adding the force arm would reach ₹6,50,000, which is ₹1,50,000 over the ₹5,00,000 budget, so the arm and the CAVE (8 times the budget) are deferred.

spec.title: Fitting the lab set into ₹5,00,000
spec.aria: A top-down chain from a ₹5,00,000 budget: buy the ₹1,50,000 stereo monitor leaving ₹3,50,000, add the ₹3,00,000 head display leaving ₹50,000, then the ₹2,00,000 force arm takes the total to ₹6,50,000, which is ₹1,50,000 over budget, so the arm and the ₹40,00,000 CAVE are deferred.

examples.question: A lab has ₹5,00,000. It must support (a) six students viewing one walkthrough together, (b) one student doing fine stereo work at a desk, and (c) one student rehearsing a surgical task needing head motion and hand force. Options: stereo monitor ₹1,50,000 (one user, no head motion, 1920×1080 total); head-mounted display ₹3,00,000 (one user, head motion, 2160×2160 per eye, about 20 pixels per degree); force-feedback arm ₹2,00,000; CAVE ₹40,00,000. Choose a set inside the budget and state what is deferred.
steps: Budget B = 5,00,000 rupees. CAVE cost = 40,00,000 rupees. CAVE / B = 40,00,000 / 5,00,000 = 8, so the CAVE is 8 times the budget. Drop it for requirement (a).

Requirement (a) needs six simultaneous viewers. The only listed device that serves six is the CAVE at 40,00,000 rupees. It is out of budget, so group viewing is deferred; the monitor is a one-user device. Requirement (b) needs fine stereo at a desk with no head motion. Use the stereo monitor: 1,50,000 rupees. Remaining = 5,00,000 − 1,50,000 = 3,50,000 rupees.

Requirement (c) needs head motion and hand force. The head-mounted display provides head motion, about 20 ppd per eye, for one user. Add it: 1,50,000 + 3,00,000 = 4,50,000 rupees. Remaining = 5,00,000 − 4,50,000 = 50,000 rupees. The hand force still needs the arm.

Add the force arm: 4,50,000 + 2,00,000 = 6,50,000 rupees. This is 6,50,000 − 5,00,000 = 1,50,000 rupees over budget. Defer the arm to next year. Group viewing for six is also deferred because the CAVE is 8 times the budget.
examples.answer: Buy the stereo monitor and the head-mounted display for 4,50,000 rupees, leaving 50,000 rupees. Requirement (b) is met, and the head-motion part of (c) is met. Defer the force-feedback arm because the full set costs 6,50,000 rupees, which is 1,50,000 rupees over the 5,00,000 rupee budget. Defer group viewing for six because the only six-user device, the CAVE, costs 40,00,000 rupees.

combo = monitor + hmd
remaining = budget - combo
with_arm = combo + arm
over = with_arm - budget
cave_factor = cave / budget

traps: Picking the highest-specification device first. Write the task numbers and the budget first.
Swapping input and output devices. A tracker measures the head; a display shows the image.
Comparing total pixels with per-eye pixels. 1920×1080 total is not the same as 2160×2160 per eye.
Treating latency and update rate as the same. Latency is a delay in ms; update rate is images per second in Hz.
Forgetting users and hygiene. One head-mounted display serves one viewer; a shared face pad needs cleaning.

quiz.q: Name the three output channels in a VR system and give one device for each.
quiz.a: Visual: head-mounted display or monitor. Audio: headphones. Haptic: force-feedback arm or glove.

quiz.q: Why is angular resolution in pixels per degree a better comparison than total pixels for two head-mounted displays?
quiz.a: Total pixels ignores field of view. Pixels per degree gives sharpness at the eye; the same total pixels over a wider field of view gives lower ppd.

quiz.q: Budget is 2,50,000 rupees. Stereo monitor costs 1,20,000; head-mounted display costs 2,80,000; haptic arm costs 90,000. Which set fits?
quiz.a: Monitor plus arm = 1,20,000 + 90,000 = 2,10,000 rupees. Remaining = 40,000. The head-mounted display alone is 30,000 over budget.

quiz.q: A team buys one head-mounted display for a six-person demo. Which selection number did they ignore, and what is the result?
quiz.a: They ignored simultaneous users. Only one person can wear it at a time, and shared face contact adds hygiene work. A large display or several units is needed.

quiz.q: Weights: visual 0.5, haptic 0.3, audio 0.2. Device X scores 4,5,2; device Y scores 5,3,4. Compute S.
Why can a CAVE be right for six viewers but wrong for a desk hand task?
quiz.a: CAVE gives a large shared view for six users, but it is fixed, costly (40,00,000 rupees in the example) and gives no hand force. Desk hand work needs a stereo monitor plus haptic arm.

beyond: Not for the exam. New headsets use pancake optics and micro-OLED panels to cut weight; AR glasses use waveguides to overlay images. Haptic research explores ultrasonic mid-air feedback and wearable gloves. Search for 'varifocal display', 'waveguide combiner', 'mid-air haptics' and 'OpenXR output devices' to go further.
